SL005-068----:
The following description is taken E. Cody’s published account (2015): ‘The central-court tomb at Doonshaskin is sited on a slight ridge in low-lying pasture just over one km from the coast. The outlook from it is now largely restricted by high field hedges. What lay under the bushes there is portrayed in Fig. 3 where stones shown cross-hatched stand upright in the ground in their original positions. Stones shown in outline are either clearly displaced or of uncertain status. Readily apparent are two chambers lying east and west of each other and about 4.5m apart. The western chamber is some 4m long and 2.6m wide. Its northern side is formed by four stones lying end to end. A stone at the inner face of the westernmost of the four sidestones is a jamb-stone; more-or-less opposite it is another jamb-stone and this stone and two other set stones either side of a partly buried stone represent the south side of the chamber. At the east end of the chamber are two opposed jamb stones inside the lines of the chamber sides. These are entrance jambs between which access was gained to the chamber while the two jamb-stones at the west end mark a point of segmentation between the chamber and another no trace of which now remains. The eastern chamber, some 3.5m long and as much as 2.9m wide, is represented by two entrance jamb stones at its front or west end, two sides tones at the north side with a gap between them and three stones at the south side. This chamber, like the western example, is open at the rear and is but the forward example of what was at least a two-chambered gallery. The stone outlined in bold on the drawing is a lintel which originally lay on top of the entrance jambs to the eastern chamber. Between the lintel and the front of the western chamber there are a number of displaced and partly-buried stones. The upright stones of the two chambers range from about 0.25m to 0.7m in exposed height.
The court, little of which survives, is represented by three set stones, 0.25m to 0.4m high, two to the north of the entrance to the western chamber and one to the north of the entrance to the eastern chamber. These are the remains of the northern half of the court. It is expected that there was a matching semi-circular setting of court stones at the south but this is no longer apparent. It may be that some of the displaced and partly-buried stones lying between the two chambers and already referred to may have served as court stones. The gap between the fronts of the opposed chambers is 4.5m east-west and this represents the greatest width of the court. The court length, its north-south dimension, is not now known but may have been a little greater than its width. In addition to the structural stones of the two galleries and the court there are some other securely-set uprights to the north of the eastern chamber, the precise role of all of which is somewhat uncertain. One stands just outside it; three more form a slight arc aligned roughly north-west to south-east to the north of the last and to the north of these there is a line of three tallish stones. …

SL007-026----:
In pasture, located on the broad, level top of a ridge on the fertile Maugherow peninsula, with panoramic views, encompassing sea, mountains and undulating hills. At E−S the tomb overlooks the broad sweep of Drumcliff Bay, backed by a dramatic line of mountains: Benbulbin, King’s Mountain and Cope’s mountain at E−ESE, the Ballygawley Mountains at SE, the long undulating spine of the Ox Mountain’s at SE−SW, and the squat bulk of Knocknarae at S. The low outline of the Belmullet Peninsula, Co. Mayo is visible across the sea to W, and the Donegal Mountains, Slieve League and the Blue Stacks are visible in the far distance at N−NNE.
This portal tomb, named ‘Druid’s Altar’ on the OS 6-inch maps, is ruined, but remains an impressive monument. A special and unusual feature of the tomb is that one of its stones bears rock art (SL007-026001-).
The tomb is of relatively simple design. A single large portal slab defines the E side. The W side is formed of three stones, the portal stone and two much smaller stones, one of which appears to be displaced. The capstone has collapsed and overlies a prostrate slab which bears the rock art. The long axis of the tomb is oriented NNE−SSW, with the entrance at NNE marked by the two portal-stones.
The two massive upright portal-stones each have a roughly lozenge-shaped cross-section and a sloping top, and are well matched in bulk and height. They are notably different, however, in surface appearance. The E portal-stone (H 2.4m; L 2.5m; T 0.9-1.1m) is a heavily quartzite-bearing, white-speckled gneiss, with a rough, seamed surface; its top comes to a peak at the NE end and slopes markedly down from there towards the back of the tomb. The W portal-stone (H 2.6m; L 1-1.1m: T 1.1.) appears to have been deliberately split, giving it relatively smooth, flat angular surfaces.
The positioning of the portal-stones is such that the gap between them narrows from the exterior (Wth 1.3m) to the interior (Wth 0.6m), creating a funnel-like access to the tomb interior.
The long E portal is the only stone on the E side of the tomb. The W side, however, is defined by the tall portal-stone and a squat, upright boulder (H 0.7m; L 0.7m; T 0.5m) which abuts its S side, with another stone (L 0.9m; Wth 0.55m; T 0.2), probably displaced, immediately to S. The latter underlies a large prostrate slab (L c. 1.7m E−W; c. 1.3m; T 0.5-0.55m), which bears rock art (SL007-026001-) in the form of a series of cupmarks on its NE side. The original position of this stone is uncertain. It now underlies the massive capstone, and one possibility is that it originally served as a back stone to support the capstone. The capstone (L 3.4m NE-SW) is an angular sandstone slab, with a rough, corroded surface. It narrows markedly from its NE end (Wth 0.85m) towards a broad mid-section and SW end (Wth 2m). It has slipped from its original position and tilts to W, with its SW end slumped heavily onto the ground.
Ground surface in the tomb interior forms a low earth and stone mound, rising 0.3-0.5m above surrounding field level. …

In pasture, located in the NE quadrant of a modern rectilinear field. Ground falls gradually to S, towards the N shoreline of Drumcliff Bay. There is a portal tomb (MA007-026----) 200m to NE.
This standing stone is not indicated on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps. A squat, flat-topped six-sided granite boulder (1.05m E−W; 0.85m N−S; H 1.4m) set upright in the ground. There is no evidence that the stone is shaped or worked; the hexagonal shape is natural, and the angular sides vary in width (Wth 0.45-0.65m). The top is relatively flat but with an uneven surface. The date and function of the stone is uncertain. It is known locally as the ‘Fairy stone’ (SMR file). The stone is used as a scratching post by farm stock and as a result some of the angles are rubbed smooth. A number of small and medium-sized field stones are piled on top of the stone.

SL007-040001-:
Situated on a lawn in the rear garden of a dwelling. Four upright and three prostrate stones appear to represent the last vestiges of a megalithic tomb. The stone to the S is 0.7m long, 0.5m thick and 1.15m high. A pair of stones, probably originally one stone, stand 2.2m to the N of this. The taller stone is 0.95m long, 0.25m thick and 0.90m high and at its N base is a smaller piece, 0.3m long by 0.18m thick and 0.45m high. Beside these to the N is a prostrate stone, 1.25m long by 0.9m wide and 0.4m thick. It is possible that this represents part of the previous stone that has been broken off. Some 0.4m W of this slab is another upright, 1.05m long, 0.55m thick and 0.8m high. A prostrate slab (0.95m by 0.80m and 0.2m thick) lies c. 3.8m to the NNW. Another prostrate slab (1.5m by 0.85m and at least 0.22m thick) lies 1.2m E of the S upright. The relationship of these to the structure is unclear and they clearly are displaced. Inasmuch as the garden has been landscaped there is no evidence of any surviving mound around the structure. The monument appears to be the last vestiges of a megalithic tomb, though in view of the scantiness of the remains some caution is necessary. The orientation of the three principal uprights would support interpretation as the remains of a gallery aligned E-W with possible affinities to those of the wedge-tomb class. However, elucidation of the full design of the monument must await excavation. Immediately E of the monument is a ring-barrow (SL007-040002-) the outline of which is visible as slight circular undulations (diam. 6.5-7m) in the ground surface.

SL012-127----:
Situated in a shallow valley into which a stream feeds from the S and forms a large pool to the SW of the monument. The ground rises to the S and N and there are limited views from the monument to E and W. The remains consist of a sub-circular cairn (c. 17.50m NNE-SSW and c. 21m WNW-ESE; averaging between 0.7m and 1m high) which is delimted by a kerb of boulders, seventeen of which appear to be in situ with many others displaced around the perimeter. The kerb is absent along the NW side and there is a gap in it at the E. The interior is composed of small stones which are covered with a thin layer of soil and vegetation. A raised bank-like feature runs N-S tangential to the cairn on its W side and incorporates a number of the kerb-stones. It expands at each end into a mound-like terminal: that on the S appears as an extension of the cairn. The precise nature of this feature is unclear as is its relationship to the cairn. The remains have clear affinities with the boulder-circle monuments within the Carrowmore passage-tomb cemetery and interpretation as a possible example of this class would not be inconsistent with the present evidence. This, however, is purely tentative and a proper elucidation of the monument must await further investigation. (Timoney 2015)

Located on the summit of Knocknarae Mountain, which is flanked to N by Sligo Bay and to SW by Ballysadare Bay. It is 85m N of the massive cairn/passage tomb (SL014-076003-), known as Maeve’s Cairn.
Indicated as ‘Carn’ on the OS 6-inch map.
A circular cairn (diam. 10-12m; H 1m) encloses a cruciform tomb built of orthostats or upright slabs. The tomb consists of a passage, with entrance at SE, which leads to a tripartite chamber. The chamber and the passage are greatly ruined and roofless; only nine orthostats of limestone and gneiss remain in situ. The limestone cairn is low, reaching only to the top of the orthostats; it has been suggested that it may never have covered the top of the chamber (Bergh 1995, 237). The cairn is encircled at a distance of c. 5m by a concentric bank (diam. 30m; Wth 4.5m; H 0.6m) of limestone. The tomb appears to have been one of several monuments on Knocknarae which were disturbed/’investigated’ in the early 1800’s by Richard Chamber Walker, a local landowner and antiquarian; Wood-Martin (1895, 660 ) recorded that burnt human and animal bones and small round unperforated beads [possibly stone] were found. (Bergh 1995, 87-8; 236-7, site 1). This is a National Monument (No. 153) in state ownership.

This massive circular, limestone cairn (diam. c. 60m; H c. 10m), named ‘Miosgan Meva’ (Maeve’s Cairn) on the OS 6-inch maps, crowns the summit of Knocknarae Mountain. Its flat-topped silhouette is a miniature version of the squat bulk of the mountain itself, which rises abruptly from the fertile coastal grasslands of the Cúil Irra peninsula, flanked by Ballysadare Bay to S and Sligo Bay to N. It is one of the most iconic archaeological monuments and landmarks in NW Ireland, its importance, past and present, manifest in the enduring folk tradition which identifies it as the burial site of the legendary Queen Maeve of Connacht.
The pale-grey cairn, rising above the dark heather-covered plateau and light-reflecting limestone escarpments of the mountain, is visible and instantly recognisable from many widespread points in the surrounding landscape. The location of the cairn itself affords panoramic views, encompassing extensive areas of county Sligo, and stretching far into counties Mayo and Donegal. Important distant landmarks which tie the cairn into an ancient network of routeways and a wider ritual and mythological landscape, include Benbulben, the cairn-topped peaks of the Ballygawley Mountains (SL020-128----; SL020-129----; SL021-007----) and the Ox Mountains (SL019-174001; SL019-174002-; SL019-177----), Cairns Hill (SL014-231001-; SL014-232----), Carrowkeel Megalithic cemetery (MA040-086---- to MA040-105----) and Kesh Corann (SL040-008----).
In its more immediate vicinity, the cairn is the dominant visual focus of a remarkably dense concentration of prehistoric ritual and settlement monuments. It is flanked on the summit by a roughly N-S linear cluster of smaller satellite tombs, cairns and mounds (SL014-076001- to SL014-076009-; SL014-076019-); the descending terraces of the mountain host huts sites (SL014-076047- to SL014-076050-), and field walls (SL014-076011-), and two caves (SL014-288----; SL014-290----) on the W flank of the mountain have produced evidence of Neolithic burials. At the foot of the mountain, the numerous passage tombs of Carrowmore megalithic cemetery (SL014-209001- , etc.), and associated monuments, spread eastwards across the undulating lowlands of Cúil Irra.
Flat-topped, with broadly sloping sides, the cairn presents a deceptively simple outline. Closer examination reveals more complexity (Berg 1995, 238-239). Although the body of the cairn is primarily limestone, a number of large gneiss boulders protrude from the perimeter at N−NE, and may be part of a kerb. Five small, low subcircular or D-shaped cairn-like concentrations of stone (diam. 8-11m; H 0.5-1m) abut the base of the cairn at E, S and W. Two large stones, a prostrate limestone slab 2m to N of the cairn, and a gneiss erratic 5.5m to S of the cairn, appear to represent deliberately placed markers on a N−S alignment. SL014-076005-:
On the summit of Knocknarae Mountain, located 35m S of a large passage tomb, known as Maeve’s Cairn (MA014-076003-), and 7m to SW of a mound (MA014-076004-).
 ‘Stone circles (site of)’ is marked at roughly this location on the OS 6-inch map. There are scant remains of this possible passage tomb. An arc of eleven low gneiss stones (H 0.1-0.3m) appears to define the S perimeter of a stone circle (diam. c. 12m) (Bergh 1995, 240), or possibly a kerb (Ó Nuallain 1989), although no trace of a cairn is evident. To N of the arc, a single set boulder may be the in situ back stone of a chamber that opened to the SE. Three displaced boulders lie to E of it. It is likely that this is one of the monuments on Knocknarae, which were disturbed in the early 1800’s by Richard Chamber Walker, a local landowner and antiquarian. (Bergh 1995, 240, site 5). This is a national monument (No. 153) in state care.

Located on a low N-S elevation, on the summit of Knocknarae Mountain, 52m SW of a large passage tomb, known as Maeve’s Cairn (MA014-076003-), and 31m to SW of a possible passage tomb (MA014-076005-).
An irregular cluster of eight boulders (av. Size c. 1.1m x 0.7m) appear to represent the very ruined remnants of a chamber, now partly concealed by heather. On the W side of the cluster, there are two recumbent split boulders (H 0.5m), aligned NNW−SSE, which may represent the SW side of the chamber. No race of a cairn or enclosing stone circle is evident. This is likely to be one of the monuments on Knocknarae, which was disturbed in the early 1800’s by Richard Chamber Walker, a local landowner and antiquarian. (Bergh 1995, 240, site 6). On the summit of Knocknarae Mountain, located 60m S of a large passage tomb, known as Maeve’s Cairn (MA014-076003-), and 18m to S of a possible passage tomb (MA014-076005-). There are two cairns (MA014-076008-; MA014-076008-) located 8m to SSW and 30m to SE respectively.
There are scant remains of this possible passage tomb. It was described by Wood-Martin (1888, 111) as ‘…a ruined circle, of which eight stones only, and four of the cist, now remain…’. It is evident now as a loose, irregular cluster of twelve gneiss boulders, with only one boulder set upright (H 0.7m). It may have been disturbed in the early 1800’s by Richard Chamber Walker, a local landowner and antiquarian. (Bergh 1995, 241). This is a National Monument (No. 153) in state ownership.

SL014-076019-:
On a broad terrace below and to SE of the summit of Knocknarae Mountain, 325m SSE of the large passage tomb, known as Maeve’s Cairn (MA014-076003-). It is located 15m from the edge of the terrace, where there is a steep fall of ground to SE.
This passage tomb consists of a circular cairn (diam. 13.5m) which encloses a central cruciform chamber and passage (L 5.5m), opening to SE. The chamber and passage, constructed of upright stones or orthostats (H 0.3-0.7m), are  now roofless, and the passage is greatly ruined. The cairn is low with a flat profile, and does not rise above the top of the orthostats. It is defined on its perimeter by a kerb of set stones (av. L 0.5-0.7m; H 0.4m). Interestingly, all the visible kerb stones and orthostats are of gneiss, bar one limestone orthostat in the back recess of the chamber. The tomb is largely concealed by heather. (Bergh 1995, 241-242, site 10).

This tomb was excavated between 1996 and 1998 as part of the Swedish Archaeological Excavations campaign at Carrowmore. The excavations have shown that 'that the tomb was in use at the same time as the Carrowmore cemetery. An intact deposition layer inside the chamber, excavated during 1997, has produced a date of around 4000 BC . . .' The tomb has produced large quantities of unburned human bones, as well as stone and bone artefacts. All the burials found in tomb were inhumations. The finds included extraordinary pieces of chert artefacts, mainly leaf-shaped or pointed arrow-heads. (Burenhult 1998)

Located in a low-lying drumlin valley with views onto the Ox Mountains in the S and Knocknarea in the W. Comprises a circular area (diam. 45m) enclosed by two banks and intervening fosse. The entrance (Wth 8.2m) is located in the E. Excavations in advance of road construction revealed a cremation at the base of the fosse and features in the interior that included a pit (diam. 1.3m; D 0.70m) and a number of cut features. Lithics that included scrapers, flakes, a chalk ball and a sherd of plain coarseware were also retrieved from the fosse. Radio-carbon dates obtained from charcoal samples produced a date of 2460-2140 cal. BC which is thought to date from the primary phase of the site (Danaher, E. 2007, 43-59).

SL014-231----:
The following description of the monument has been published by Bergh (1995, 232-3): ‘Located on the flat summit of Cams Hill. The site consists of a cairn with a diameter of 45-49 m and a height of c. 5 m. The flat top is slightly hollowed. A rich vegetation of briars covers the summit of the hill, but this vegetation ceases at a distance of c. 10 m from the cairn, and this area as well as the cairn as such, is covered by grass. Extensive quarrying has been made within the site and especially on the N. and W. sides. The perimeter of the cairn is however relatively untouched, as the quarrying seems to mainly have been made from the upper edges of the cairn, which is evident from the remaining part of the flat top.
Dimensions: Diameter, 45-49 m. Estimated original diameter, c. 43 m. Height, 5 m (present, as well as original).
The diameter of 43 m is calculated from the about 25 kerbstones present along the perimeter of the cairn in SW. It is notable that nearly all of the visible kerbstones are found at, or very close to, the present edge of the cairn. Evidently the slip of the cairn has not been extensive. The present height is considered to coincide with the original height, as no material seems to have been removed from the dished top.
Stones used within the construction: The cairn consists of locally available limestone, while gneiss has been used for kerbstones, the internal stone revetment, dry-walling, as well as within the two small cairns on the E. and W sides of the main cairn.
Kerbstones: About 25 kerbstones are visible within the site, and nearly all are on the SW side of the cairn. These stones measure c. 0.8 x 0.6m, and all arc gneiss. The have been placed recumbent on the ground with their long-axis forming the perimeter of the cairn.
Internal stone revetment: 15 stones have been recorded c. 3m inside the kerb in SW, describing a curved line parallel to the perimeter of the cairn. These stones measure c.0.5 x 0.4m, and all are gneiss which is in contrast with the limestone-built cairn. These 15 stones most likely represent an internal stone revetment which most likely continues all around the monument, even though it can only be traced for a length of c.15 in the SW part of the cairn.
Dry-walling: On the N. side of the cairn, a drystone walling can be followed for c.5m. The stones in the dry-walling are gneiss field stoncs, with a size of c. 0.3 - 0.4m. The present height of the dry-walled section is c. 0.4m.
Exterior Features
Bank (?): Along the base of the cairn, mainly on its east side, there seems to be a low bank with a height of only c. 0.3m and a width of c. 4m. It cannot be stated with certainty whether this bank is a part of the original construction or if it is a result of a cairn slip.
Platform (?): On the south side a low platform runs along the base of the cairn from SE to SW and its outer edge is parallel to the perimeter of the cairn. The width of the platform is about 9m and its height c. 0.3m. At its western end the outer part of the platform transforms into a bank with a width of c. 2m and a height of c. 0.4m. This bank runs for a distance of c. 10m and then ends in a U-shaped curve into the cairn. …

SL014-232----:
This large cairn, a possible passage tomb, is a National Monument in State ownership (no. 568). The following description of the monument has been published by Bergh (1995, 232): ‘The site is the easternmost of the two [see SL014-231----] and overlooks the Garavogue River, 700m to the east. The site consists of a large, flat-topped cairn with a diameter of 53-58m, and a height of c. 7.5m. The cairn is placed at the northern end of a ridge that forms the summit. The hillside declines close to the cairn on all sides except to the S where the ground is level. Immediately to the W of the cairn there is a fairly steep, but short slope of only c. 3m, and the cairn has evidently on purpose been placed along this edge. The site is situated in a deciduous forest and is not visible until one is nearly at it. It is today wholly covered by a rich vegetation of bushes and smaller trees. This thick vegetation is probably the reason why the plan of the cairn never has been recorded before, and it definitely was the reason to why it was not measured by Wood-Martin according to the following: “Its circumference at base could not be ascertained, owing both to the uneven nature of the ground and to its being surrounded by trees, and a close undergrowth of briars, furze, & c.” (Wood-Martin 1888, p. 123). Minor quarrying seems to have taken place in the SE part of the cairn, and on the flat top there are several hollows and depressions which are the remains of earlier diggings into the cairn. A number of small semi-circular stone walls are present within the site, and are most likely of modem date.
Dimensions: Diameter, 53m (present minimum diameter/original maximum diameter). Height, 7.5m (present and original). Diameter of top, 23m (present maximum diameter).
The diameter of the cairn is 53m in N-S, but 58m in E-W. The slip of the cairn seems to vary, and has probably been greatest towards the W due to the short but steep slope here. The E and S sides of the cairn are the best
preserved, and the diameter of 53m is considered as being a maximum for the original diameter The flat and slightly hollowed top has a maximum diameter of 23m. The ground level outside the cairn is 2m higher on the S and E, than on the N and W sides of the cairn. The absolute height of the cairn is c. 7.5m.’ (Bergh 1995, 232, Fig. 30).
Another cairn/possible passage tomb, very similar in size and construction, is located on a hilltop c. 400m to SW.

Shown as 'stone circle' on the OS 6 inch map (1913). Wood-Martin (1887-8, 256-7) describes the site as a slightly raised mound 'c. 57' N-S by 45' E-W '; 'formerly encircled with boulders'. He records that the site was traditionally called 'Coolcrave' and was said to be the burial place of those who died in a battle which took place nearby. The extant remains consist of a semi-circular level area, c. 18m N-S. defined on the NW-E-S by remnants of a ring of close-set boulders and incorporated into a curving field wall on the S-E and NE. The stones survive best in the NW-N where six to seven boulders occur in a curving line. In the S five close set boulders appear also to be in situ and a there are a few isolated stones protruding from the overgrowth on the E. The boulders have a maximum dimension of 0.50m-0.70m, and vary in height from 0.40m to 0.80m. The W half of the site has been obliterated and on this side the site is now bordered by a rough track immediately to the W from which the ground falls away sharply. (Bergh 1995, 219, 222)

Towards the N end and highest point of relatively flat-topped Doomore Mountain. The site overlooks Ballysadare Bay and commands a magnificent outlook in all directions. This is a circular cairn (diam. 21m; H c. 2m) the perimeter of which is under peat-grown heather. Towards the western edge of the flat top of the cairn there is a roughly constructed heap of stones, circular in plan (diam. 7m; H 1.5m). The age and purpose of this feature is uncertain but it may be a 19th-century OS trigonometrical station. Just E of the centre of the cairn there is a 20th-century OS concrete-built trigonometrical pillar. At the NNE a line of four large stones extends towards the centre of the cairn from a point c. 3m inside the perimeter. These stones, which are substantially buried, are of uncertain status but could represent tomb structure, possibly a passage tomb. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 94)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Situated on the E side of a peat-covered plateau on Knockachree Mountain in the Ox Mountains at an altitude of c. 538m OD. The ground falls away sharply c. 20m to the E of the monument. The views to the N to SSW are restricted due to peat banks along horizon, but there are excellent views in all other directions with the Bricklieves, Knocknashee, Knocknarea, Croagh Patrick and the E Ox Mountain range clearly visible.
The remains consist of a roughly circular cairn (c. 16.8m E-W; 17.2m N-S) that is partially buried in peat, especially along the E and SE sectors. Its highest point is c. 2.6m from SE edge. The cairn is best preserved in the SW quadrant and there is a considerable amount of cairn slippage along the E side: two OS trigonometrical stations, consisting of small circular heaps of stones (diam. 1.5-2m; H 0.7-1m), were built on its highest points. The N sector of the cairn has been quarried out exposing an area c. 8m (N-W) by 5m (E-W). Four possible kerbstones are visible along this N edge and three possible orthostats are exposed near the centre of this area.

The centre stone is the tallest (H 1.7m; 0.8m x 0.55m) and its long axis is transverse to the alignment of the row. The SSW stone (H 0.6m; 0.6m x 0.6m) is also upright. Inside the SW edge of a graveyard (SL020-171002-). An upright rectangular limestone pillar (H 0.9m; Wth 0.5m; T 0.26m; long axis NNW-SSE). Small moss-covered stones are piled around its base. O'Rorke ([1889], vol. 2, 247) recorded that the stone, popularly known as 'Clogh an Easpuig' [the Bishop's stone], marks the resting place of a bishop and, according to local tradition, the part of it which is sunken in the ground is ogham-inscribed. A small roughly oval stone (L 0.3m; Wth 0.25m; T 0.7m) lies at the base of the E face of the pillar. It has a flat base and a slightly rounded upper surface which contains five shallow circular holes with rounded bottoms (diam. 0.02m; D 0.03-0.05m) which, according to local tradition, were used to hold candles.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

SL020-181----:
Some 2km S of Ballysadare Bay on the narrow summit of Croaghaun Mountain which commands an extensive outlook in all directions. A SE-facing undifferentiated passage tomb of rectangular outline (L 1.7m; Wth 0.95m) stands in a circular cairn (diam. 7m; H. c. 0.6m). Three stones form the left-hand side of the structure, one stone of a probable original three stands at the right-hand side and it is closed by a backstone. A sillstone stands at the front of the chamber. The site was excavated in 1985 (Bergh 1986, 35; Bergh 1995, 104-5, 225). Cremated human bone was found in the chamber and also a fragment of a poppy-headed antler/bone pin, one piece of chert with wear-marks and fragments of a coarse ware pottery. Five minor deposits of cremated bone were found in the cairn with one of which there were sherds of food vessel type. A hollow scraper made of chert was also found in the cairn. During the excavation two displaced slabs, likely to have been chamber roofstones, were found S and W of the structure. Radiocarbon dating of charcoal from an in situ cremation suggest it was deposited in the interval 5640 to 5490 BC (calendar years). This date is much earlier than would be expected for a passage-tomb so it may be that charcoal already many centuries old somehow became associated with the burial deposit. Charcoal associated with cremated bone in another part of the chamber has been dated to the interval 4675-4460 cal. BC. This date too, according to the excavator, presents 'problems of interpretation'. A prehistoric wall (Wth 3-8m; H c. 1m; L c. 175m) (SL020-182----) of large boulders, which may have been associated with the passage tomb, lies c. 130m to S where it curves around the base of the mountain roughly SE-SW (Bergh 1986, 34-5). (Ó Nualláin 1989, 93-4)

SL020-233----:
In the N part of a modern rectangular pasture field, on a level terrace on a N-facing slope, which provides good views NW-E: Knocknarae draws the eye to NW, Benbulbin and the Dartry Mountains define the skyline to N, and the Ballygawley Mountains are visible to E. Ground rises gently for c. 15m to SE-S to a low E-W ridge.
This record refers to an unclassified megalithic tomb first recorded in the late 1800’s by Wood-Martin (1887-8, 260-1), who described it as an 'elongated cist, apparently divided into four septa or compartments. Its longer axis, measuring about 25 feet [7.6m], is approximately E. and W., its average width being 15 feet [4.5m]’. He noted that ‘the few Irish-speaking natives in the vicinity called it “Tumban” (i.e. little tumulus’)’.
Wood-Martin mentioned that Seaton F. Milligan ‘had made a slight excavation, and found some bones seemingly bearing traces of fire; but on his return early in the following week, to complete his exploration, he found that the country-people had employed themselves on the previous Sunday in digging in the interior of the monument, thereby displacing several of the stones.’ He added that ‘the debris thrown out of the interior was examined, but nothing came under notice save a few calcined and uncalcined bones and a piece of quartz.’ (Ibid. 61).
The tomb is not indicated on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps and Wood-martin did not record its exact location. According to local information, it stood c. 200m N of a cashel (MA020-123----), and the chamber walls with a single in situ capstone were still extant in the 1980’s (pers. comm. Ivan Sullivan, 2023). In the late 1980’s the tomb was removed during land reclamation works and the stones are said to have been dumped in a heap close to the W boundary of the field at ITM 568566 830680 c. 100m S of their original position. A heap of stones is still visible at that location, including eight large irregular-shaped boulders (size range: 0.5m by 0.8m to 1m by 1.8m) with a number of smaller boulders and a scatter of small loose rubble.
There are now no visible structural remains of the tomb at its original location. A few shallow indentations (c. 0.8-1m across) in the grassy field surface may indicate the original position of the stones, and it is possible that subsurface remains survive as the 1980’s land reclamation works did not involve deep excavation (pers. comm. Ivan Sullivan, 2023).
Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy
Date of upload: 30 May 2023
SL020-274----:
Sited alongside a trackway in extensive woodland in a gap in the Ox Mountains 0.7km NW of Ballygawley Lough. There are a number of mature deciduous trees on the site and the stumps of others. To N and W the ground drops quite sharply to a stream that flows NW-SE. Trees inhibit the outlook from the site but Maeve's cairn on Knocknarea is visible to the NNW. A ring of boulders (19.5m N-S, 17.5m E-W) encompasses a slight platform. There are a number of gaps in the ring of boulders but the indications are that they were contiguously placed. Among the numerous gaps are two that may be original features, one at the SE (Wth 1.3m) and another at the NW (Wth 1.1m). A number of prostrate boulders outside the perimeter may be displaced. Some of the boulders encircling the platform are quite sizeable (the largest is 0.95m x 0.85m x 1.15m high) but others are noticeably smaller. The tops of at least three stones are visible about 3m inside the perimeter at the W. The status of these is quite unclear but their presence suggests that there may have been an inner ring of stones. Somewhat to the W of the centre of the enclosed area four stones lie prostrate. The larger two are about 1.6m and 1.4m in maximum dimensions. These may represent some form of internal feature. The nature of the site is somewhat uncertain but it may be a Carrowmore-type passage tomb. It is indicated as a small oval field on the 1913 OS 6-inch map. Some 100m to the W there is another possible passage tomb (SL020-275----).
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

SL020-275----:

A gapped line (L c. 17m) large boulders forms an incomplete ring SE-NW. The nature of the site is somewhat uncertain but it may be a Carrowmore-type passage tomb. Some 100m to the E there is a another possible passage tomb (SL020-274----).

SL021-019----:
On a knoll in good pasture c. 150m E of Lough Dargan and c. 500m WSW of a court tomb (SL021-020----) at Carrownagh. The tomb stands in a low, oval mound (28m E-W; 12.5m N-S; max. H 1.5m). A largely destroyed full court (L 7.5m) at the E leads to a gallery (L 6m; max. Wth 2.7m). Two jambs define the entrance to the gallery and two more divide it into two chambers. The court is represented by five stones, one flanking each entrance jamb and three at its outer end. A gap between two of three outer stones may form the entrance to the court. A large stone standing on edge at the inner end of the court may have rested on the entrance jambs as a lintel. The gallery sides are intact save for a gap at the inner half of the N side of the front chamber. There are two displaced stones in this chamber. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 50-51, no. 78)

On a rocky rise, in rush-grown pasture. This unclassified megalithic tomb is a National Monument in State ownership (no. 277). An orthostat (L 1.3m; T 0.3m; H 1.3m if upright) aligned SW-NE and leaning to the S is the only set stone here. In addition four large slabs lie at the site. One (max. dim. 2.7m) adjoins the NE end of the orthostat and beyond this is another slab of similar size. Immediately S of the orthostat there is a large slab (max. dim. 2m) and alongside this to the SW there is another. There are also seven smaller prostrate stones at the site. The stones seem to represent the remains of a megalithic tomb or perhaps an abandoned attempt to build one (Ó Nualláin 1989, 53, no. 83). The presence of two large slabs one resting above the other some 15m to the S is cited as support for the view that construction of the monument may not have been completed. A court tomb (SL021-104----) lies c. 50m to ENE.

SL021-104----:
On a poorly drained low-lying patch of ground about 50m ENE of an unclassified megalithic tomb (SL021-062----).
This court tomb is a National Monument in State ownership (no. 277). The inner end of a SSE-facing gallery (L 4m; max. Wth 2.6m) is divided by segmenting jambs inset in the gallery walls into a well-preserved rear chamber (L c. 2m) and an outer chamber now represented by two opposed sidestones. The status of an upright stone between these two sidestones and crossing the gallery is unclear. Some 2m to the W of the gallery there is a lone kerbstone and 2-3m E of the gallery there are three others. The alignment of these kerbstones suggest that the structure stood in a cairn of trapezoidal plan. There is some cairn fill in the gallery and between it and the kerbstones. There are a number of displaced stones at the site including a group of four large examples just S of the surviving gallery structure. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 53-4, no. 84)

SL024-005----:
In rough upland pasture, in the Ox Mountains, located on a small ridge or knoll, flanked immediately to N and S by two small, boggy valleys. The knoll is cloaked in blanket bog, with ground cover of moorland grasses, sedges, rushes and mosses, broken by areas of gneiss outcropping. To E ground falls away to the shore of Easkey Lough, overshadowed on its E side by the high main ridge of the Ox Mountains; to W there is a drop to a broad, flat expanse of blanket bog which stretches far to W and NW. The standing stone consists of an upright, narrow flat-topped pillar of schist. It has naturally rounded edges, giving it a roughly oval cross-section (0.2m E–W; 0.12-0.15m N–S). It leans slightly to N so that its vertical height is 0.6m, and the leaning or oblique dimension is 0.75m. There is at least a further 0.5m of the stone embedded in the peat.

SL025-002----:
On rocky reclaimed pasture below the steeper S slopes of the Ox Mountains and commanding an extensive outlook to the S. A layer of peat covers parts of the structure.
This wedge tomb is a National Monument in State ownership (no. 523). A well-preserved gallery opens onto a façade and an outer wall. The gallery, facing WNW, is divided by two jamb-like stones inset in the gallery walls and a septal-stone, now in a displaced position just E of them, into a portico (L 1.4m; Wth 1.3m) and main chamber (L 6m; Wth at front 1.6m, at mid-length 2.15m, at rear 0.7m). A single stone forms each side of the portico. There are eight stones on the N side of the main chamber and seven on the S side. There is a small stone immediately outside the easternmost stone at the S. The E end of the structure is covered by three overlapping roofstones resting on the gallery sides. A large stone is interposed between either end of the westernmost roofstone and the top of the S side of the gallery. Outer-walling survives beyond both the sides and back of the gallery. There are ten outer-wall stones at the N, twelve at the S, and a single large orthostat is in position at the E end of the monument. There is a set stone of uncertain function 0.7m outside the E end of the outer-walling at the N. A single facade-stone links the outer wall at the N to the front of the portico. Its counterpart at the S is now prostrate. There is considerable cairn material between the outer-walling and the gallery but no trace of a mound outside the structure. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 54-5, no. 86)

SL025-008----:
On top of a ridge in rolling drumlin-like country. A well-preserved gallery (L 8.9m), flanked at both sides by the remains of outer-walling, opens onto a flat facade at the W. The front of the monument is incorporated in a field fence. The gallery is divided by a septal-stone into a portico (L 1.6m; Wth 1.4m) and main chamber (L 7m; Wth 1.7m at septal-stone, 1m near the backstone). Single stones form the sides of the portico and each articulates with a facade-stone. A stone stands in the gap between the facade-stones thus dividing the gallery entrance. Eight stones are in position on the N side of the main chamber and six on the S side and these display a general decrease in height from W to E. A roofstone covers the portico and another the rear of the gallery. Between these three others lie displaced along the gallery. A line of three outer-wall stones (the middle one fallen outwards) adjoins the northern facade-stone and a lone outer-wall stone remains on the opposite side of the structure about 1m beyond the front of the main chamber. Outside this there is a displaced slab and there is another outside the N side of the gallery. There is an unclassified megalithic tomb (SL025-009----) c. 300m to SE. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 55-6, no. 87)

SL025-009----:
The monument, greatly ruined, stands about 300m SE of a wedge tomb (SL025-008----) and is on similar land at the foot of the ridge occupied by that tomb. It consists of a number of large prostrate slabs and leaning stones along with some small set stones. The remains stretch some 7.5m SE-NW, perhaps the alignment of the ruined structure, and are described here as if they lay E-W. There are two set stones at the W end neither more than 0.8m long or 0.2m high, one set transversely to the long axis of the structure and the other at its more northerly side. Close to the E end there is a large westwards-leaning slab (L 2.3m; H if upright c. 2m) at right angles to the long axis of the structure. West of and at right angles to the S end of this there is a somewhat smaller northwards-leaning slab. At right-angles to the outer face of the former there is a small set stone (L 0.6m; T 0.15m; H 0.25m) and 0.6m S of the latter there is another (L 0.9m; T 0.15m; H 0.4m). Along the N side of structure there are three large displaced slabs, the largest 3.5m x 2.4m x 0.6m T. There are also other smaller displaced and partly buried stones at the site. Traces of mound survive along the N side and W end of the structure. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 56, no. 88)

SL025-022----:
At the foot of a NW-facing slope and close to a stream in damp pasture. The structure is damaged and difficult to interpret. The main feature is an uphill- and E-facing chamber (L 4m; Wth c. 2m) with its back to the stream. A large stone (H c. 1.5m) forms each side and it is closed by an inset backstone (L 1.8m; min. T 0.3m; H 1.4m), the jagged top of which indicates it has been broken. In front of the northern sidestone there is the stump of another orthostat (L 1.6m; min. H 1.7m) possibly a broken portal-stone. Part of its detached upper portion lies at the front of the chamber. Some low stones just N of the stump of this orthostat are part of an old field fence. A large flat slab (4m x 3m; T 0.4m), a displaced roofstone, leans against the outer face of the southern sidestone. Both sidestones lean to the S and both are split. There is considerable grass-grown fill in the chamber. The tomb must remain unclassified but its location, facing uphill away from a stream, the use of a single large stone for each side of the chamber, and the presence of a great roofstone would suggest it may be a ruined portal-tomb.
Five metres W of the chamber there is a large prostrate slab (2.45m x 2.5m; T 0.4m), its W end raised clear of the ground where it rests on a set stone (L 1.1m; H 0.55m; T 0.15m). There are other partly buried slabs here. The indications are that this may have been some form of chamber. Some 7m to the N there is another large prostrate slab (4m x 2.4m; max. T 0.4m).

SL025-154----:
On rough pasture on the lower slopes of the Ox Mountains commanding an outlook to the S. The tomb, well-preserved, is partly obscured by a fence running along its N side and W end. A gallery facing WSW is divided by a jamb-like stone at the N into a portico (L 1.9m) and main chamber (L 7.6m; Wth 1.55m at front, 1.95m towards mid-length, 1.3m at rear). The long axis of the gallery and that of the portico are at a slight angle to each other. A stone at the front of the portico divides the gallery entrance in two. Only one stone, at the S, remains of the portico sides. The main chamber orthostats are partly concealed by fill. Eight are visible on the N side, eleven to the S, and the gallery is closed by a single stone. A slab resting on the S side of the gallery at about mid-length seems to be a displaced roofstone. The facade and outer-walling represented by twelve orthostats merge to form a broad curve around the N side of the gallery. A large orthostat about 1m beyond the gallery backstone seems to represent the back of the outer wall. To the S, four outer-wall stones are in place beyond the middle and back of the gallery and between the easternmost of these and the large orthostat representing the back of the outer wall there are five fallen examples. SL034-208001-:
On gently rolling upland pasture about 2km to the E of the NE corner of Lough Arrow. The remains of a WSW-facing gallery (L at least 3.5m) divided by a septal-stone into a portico (L 1.5m; Wth 1.9m at the front, 1.6m at the septal-stone) and wedge-shaped main chamber, stands at the centre of a substantial circular cairn (20m N-S; 17m E-W; H 1m). Three orthostats, two together about 1.5m W of the front of the gallery and another almost 2m SE of these protrude from the cairn and seem to represent a buried kerb or outer-wall. A single stone forms each side of the portico. The septal-stone reaches to the level of the chamber sides each of which is now represented by two orthostats. Outside the junction of the two stones at each side there is a small stone apparently intended to strengthen the wall and there is another outside the end of the eastern of the two orthostats at the N side. A single roofstone resting on the septal-stone and the gallery sides covers the remains of the main chamber. A fence follows the cairn perimeter at the W and S and there is the remains of a small limekiln (SL034-208003-) at its eastern edge. The central part of the cairn, i.e. that part of it adjoining the structure rises about 1m above the rest of the cairn and includes spoil from the gallery area. This site was dug into at least twice in the 19th century and human remains, a piece of bronze and pottery sherds, among which were the remains of at least three Beakers, are among the recorded finds (Wood-Martin 1883-4, 461-2; 1888, 182-5; Madden 1969, 157-9). SL034-224----:

A gallery (L 6m; Wth 1.9m at the front) is represented by three sidestones at its front or WSW end, one on the N side and two on the S side, and by its backstone. Just 0.7m E of the two stones at the S side there is a set stone at right angles to the line of the gallery side which may have functioned as a buttress-stone though it is unusually large for that purpose. About 1m outside the northern sidestone there is an outer-wall stone and 1.3m to the E of it another. Between these and the line of the gallery side there are two more set stones. These seem to represent an intermediate line of walling between the gallery side and the outer-wall. There are a number of prostrate stones at the site. One of these adjoins the N end of the backstone and may be a fallen sidestone. Another at the NW corner of the structure might be a fallen facade-stone. A poorly preserved low mound at the site scarcely extends beyond the confines of the structure. Some uncertainty has been expressed about the classification of this tomb (Ó Nualláin 1989, 64-5, no. 104) but the available indications are that it is a wedge-tomb.

A U-shaped court (L at least 5.5m; Wth c. 7.5m) at the SSE leads to a gallery (L 9m). Three stones remain of the more easterly arm of the court and five of the opposite arm. Two jambs mark the entrance to the gallery which is divided by three other pairs of jambs into four chambers. There is a sillstone between the jambs separating the second and third chamber. The gallery sides are quite well-preserved and the backstone is in place. The tomb is in a poorly preserved long mound (L c. 33m). About 2m outside the E arm of the court there is a kerbstone and another 1.5m outside the W arm. Seven probable kerbstones are exposed along the northern half of the W side of the mound. The backstone and southern sidestone of what appears to be a small lateral subsidiary chamber stand at the W side of the mound almost 5m beyond the back of the gallery. A field fence extends along both arms of the court, the E side of the gallery and from the gallery backstone northwards along the mound. There is a small quarry to the E of this fence behind the gallery. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 66-7, no. 106)

SL035-063----:
Near the crest of a low ridge in rolling pasture. Part of a WSW-facing gallery (L c. 3m; Wth 1.2m) and the remains of outer-walling and a facade survive here. Two orthostats are visible on the S side of the gallery. Opposite the western of these there is another orthostat and to the E of this two corbels rising above fill continue the line of the gallery side. Just beyond these there is a partly concealed stone which may also be a corbel. There are five outer-wall stones to the S of the gallery, two of them together at the W and three alongside at the E. The N side of the outer-walling is represented by a single stone. Two facade stones adjoin the W end of the outer-wall at the S. Two roofstones cover the surviving length of gallery. A third roofstone which lay to the E of these and also the northern half of the façade have been lost since the later half of the 19th century (Wood-Martin 1883-4, 453-4; 1888, 172-4). A stone protruding from a fence crossing the NW corner of the structure and another alongside it may be displaced facade stones. A stone at the E end of the structure could indicate the back of the outer wall but is not definitely in situ. Traces of a mound, not more than 0.5m high, are visible along the S side of the monument. A court tomb (SL035-062----) is c. 100m to NNE and the site of an unclassified megalithic tomb (SL035-061----) is c. 150m to NNE. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 65-6, no. 105)

SL035-078----:
This destroyed monument stood on rocky pasture just over 200m W of a court tomb (SL035-079----). The tomb is marked on the 1838 OS 6-inch map but had been demolished when Wood-Martin (1883-4, 458-60, no. 20; 1888, 180-82, no. 2) visited the area later in the same century. He was informed that this tomb was similar in plan to the court tomb (SL035-079----) 200m to E. Some large stones visible in a fence at the site in 1956 may have originally formed part of the monument (Ó Nualláin 1989, 68, no. 109). An account in 1836, which seems to refer to this tomb, describes it as '... now eighteen or twenty feet [c. 6m] long, and about five feet [c. 1.5m] broad, having flags fixed around it' and claims that it had been opened some years earlier when human bones were reportedly found in it (OSL, 171-4). The report also records a claim that a 'golden breast plate' was found either in the tomb or nearby. The indications are that this destroyed monument was a court tomb.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

SL035-079----:
On rocky pasture commanding an extensive outlook to the S. This court tomb is a National Monument in state ownership (no. 465). A U-shaped open court (L c. 7m) at the NNE leads to a well-preserved gallery (L 13m; Wth 1.5-2.9m) of four chambers. There are some poorly defined traces of mound around the structure. The two entrance jambs of the gallery function as courtstones and, in addition, one orthostat of the more westerly arm of the court survives and two remain on the other side. At the outer end of this side of the court there is a low moss-covered courtstone and just beyond and at right angles to it another low stone, apparently part of the tomb facade. A stone, split in two, and set more or less along the main axis of the structure stands in the gallery entrance and divides it in two. Another stone at right angles to the last closes the eastern half of the entrance gap. The divisions between the first three chambers are marked by single jambs, in each case at the W. The third and fourth chambers are separated by a sillstone. The chamber sidestones and the backstone of the gallery survive intact. There are three blocks of stone of uncertain origin between 1m and 9m beyond the back of the gallery. A stone wall extends NE-SW across the W arm of the court. A large limestone block on top of a smaller stone lies c. 30m to SW and is known locally as the 'Rocking stone'. An unclassified megalithic tomb (SL035-078----) lies c. 200m to W. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 68-9, no. 110)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

SL035-097001-:
On sloping ground in thin-soiled pasture with an outlook to the S. The tomb stands in a subrectangular mound (19.5m N-S; 12.5m E-W) (SL035-097002-). Two possible kerbstones are exposed inside the edge of the mound at the SE and another at the NW. The tomb, which faces N, consists of the scant remains of a court represented by an entrance jamb to the E and alongside it a courtstone leading to a gallery (L 9m; Wth 2m) divided into a very short antechamber and three main chambers. A transeptal chamber opens off each side of the first main chamber and just over 2m beyond the gallery a subsidiary chamber opens to the E. A jamb just 0.4m behind the eastern entrance jamb separates the antechamber from the first main chamber. Two stones form each side of this chamber and gaps between them allow entry to the transeptal chambers, the western formed by two stones on each side and a backstone and the eastern represented by opposed stones at its inner end and a backstone. Two jambs, the eastern possibly partly displaced, separate the first main chamber from the second each side of which is formed by two stones. A long sill, flanked at either side by jambs, separates the last from the rear chamber. The W side of this chamber is formed by two stones, only the innermost orthostat survives on the E side, and it is closed by a backstone. The subsidiary chamber is represented by a backstone and two adjoining sidestones. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 69-70, no. 111)
Two previously recorded orthostats were noted in 2020: one at the N end of the W wall of the middle chamber of the gallery; the other at the W end of the N wall of the E transeptal chamber (pers. comm.  Sam Moore).
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

SL035-106----:

Wood-Martin (1883-4, 451, no. 8; 1888, 172, no. 8) states: 'It appears to have been oblong in form; it lay right in the centre of the present road, and most of the slabs of which it was composed are now in the fences on either side'. SL036-001001-:
In a small sub-circular sinkhole (E-W 26m; N-S 23m; D 2.5m along N; which presumably formed after the monument was constructed) in an area of numerous sinkholes on the bog-grown S-facing slope of the Ox Mountains (Slieve Gamph). This is a grass-grown circular cairn (diam. 11.5m to 12.5m; H c. 2m) at the top of which the upper part of the N side of a well-built drystone wall is exposed. A C-shaped arc of walling (SL036-001002-) survives and outlines a space measuring 1.7m E-W and 1m N-S. Up to four courses of walling (H 0.8m) are exposed. The wall is built of small stones laid in corbel fashion so that it inclines inwardly as it rises. The wall is part of a burial chamber the design and nature of which is uncertain. The elevated location of the site and the presence of a circular cairn suggest it might belong in the passage tomb tradition. (Aldridge 1960-1, 89-90)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

SL036-002----:
On the bog-covered plateau below the higher slopes of the Ox Mountains and commanding an extensive view S and E across the basin of the River Moy. The tomb, in an oval bog-grown cairn (20.5m E-W; max. 13m N-S; H 1.5m), consists of a gallery (L 6m; Wth 1.5-3.3m) preceded at the E by the N side of a court. Two of the courtstones adjoin the gallery entrance and four others are 1.5m to the E. The outer two of these four may represent the side of an entrance passage leading to the court which may have been quite small. The well-preserved gallery narrows to both front and rear and its sides are doubled in places. Two jambs set at an angle to each other form the entrance to the gallery and another pair, the northern of the two split into three pieces, divide it into two chambers. The site is littered with displaced stones, some of them quite large. There is a low wall around the tomb probably built with stones taken from the cairn. Another court tomb (SL036-003----) c. 300m to S and a possible megalithic tomb (SL036-002001-) c. 30m to SW. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 70-1, no. 112)

SL036-002001-:
On a bog-grown plateau below the higher slopes of the Ox Mountains and 30m SW of a court tomb (SL036-002----). Some eight stones remain of what may be a ruined gallery aligned NE-SW, possibly c. 8m long. It is exposed in a grassy hollow (c. 8m x 7m) surrounded by bog. The stones are of generally slight proportions. At the NE there is a set stone (0.4m x 0.4m; H 0.2m). Some 0.8m to the SW there is a possible sidestone (L 1m; H 0.3m) leaning against which there is another stone, possibly a displaced corbel. Immediately SW of these there is a jamb-like stone (0.55m x 0.55m; H 0.5m). Some 0.6m further to the SW a partly buried stone, possibly a split boulder (1.4m x 0.35m; H 1m), may not be in situ. Just SW of the last a thin firmly set stone (0.8m x 0.15m; H 0.6m) stands at right angles to the alignment of the structure. It could be a jamb. A set stone (0.8m x 0.1m; H 0.7m) lies 0.4m to the SW and 0.8m beyond this there is another (0.7m x 0.2m; H 0.2m).

SL036-003----:
A National Monument (No. 479) in state guardianship. On a bog-grown plateau below the higher slopes of the Ox Mountains and c. 300m S of another court tomb (SL036-002----) and on the same bog-covered plateau. The rear chamber (L 3.3m; max. Wth 2.2m) of a NE-facing court tomb is exposed at about mid-length in a bog-grown mound (L 34.5m; Wth 12m NE end, 7m SW end; H 3m). At the front of the chamber there are two jambs either side of a sill-stone. The sides, each of three orthostats, and backstone of the chamber support well-preserved corbelling which seems to extend beyond the jambs and sill into the concealed front part of the gallery. A largely concealed roofstone covers the back of the chamber. The peat cover above this is 0.6m thick. A slight depression in the mound, c. 5m from its NE end, may indicate the presence of a buried court. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 71-2, no. 113)

SL036-035----:
In a broad valley among foothills at the SW end of the Ox Mountains. It lies to the E of a field fence on land reclaimed from the bog. A well-preserved SW-facing gallery (L 8.7m) opens onto a flat facade which links it to flanking lines of outer-walling. A curved line (L c. 8m) of seven orthostats between 2m and 4m beyond the more northerly side of the outer-walling seems to represent a kerb. The whole stands in a low mound (16.5m N-S; 12m E-W; max. H 0.75m). A high septal-stone divides the gallery into a portico (L 2m; Wth 2.1m at front, 1.8m at the septal-stone) and main chamber (L 6.2m; Wth 1.6m at front, narrowing to c. 0.8m at rear). Single stones form the portico sides. The septal-stone, now split from base to top towards its N end, is inset in the gallery walls and rises 0.2m above the portico sides. Two broken and partly concealed roofstones lie to the E of the septal-stone and there are other smaller displaced stones beyond these. The N side of the main chamber is formed by eight orthostats some of which partly overlap each other. Only three stones, alongside to the W, remain of the opposite side. Ten outer-wall stones are in position to both N and S and the eastern two examples at both sides turn inwards towards the backstone of the gallery. A single façade-stone joins the front of the gallery to the outer wall at each side. Adjoining the inner end of each facade-stone is an orthostat. These two stones stand at either side of the portico entrance (Wth 0.8m). Another wedge tomb (SL036-036----) lies c. 1km to NE in the same valley. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 72-3, no. 114)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

SL036-036----:
On a little knoll in the same valley as another wedge-tomb (SL036-035----) c. 1km to SW. A WNW-facing gallery (L at least 7m; Wth 1.85m at front, narrows sharply to rear), flanked at the S by the slight remains of an outer wall, stands on a D-shaped platform (H 0.5m to 1m) which appears to be artificial. There are vague traces of mound at the back and along the N side of the gallery. A number of displaced and largely concealed roofstones cover the E end of the structure. Three orthostats are in position at the front of the more northerly side of the gallery, the first set outside the line of the other two. Beyond these, two largely concealed slabs, apparently sidestones, have collapsed inwards. About 1m beyond these another inward-leaning stone, now split, also appears to be a sidestone. Four orthostats are in position at the outer end of the more southerly side of the gallery, the second set outside the line of the others. About 1.5m beyond these an outwards-leaning stone may also be a sidestone. There are three buttress-stones outside the N side of the gallery, one at right angles to the inner end of the first orthostat and there are two just beyond the collapsed easternmost sidestone. There is another buttress-stone outside the more westerly end of the second sidestone at the S. Outside and parallel to the opposite end of the same orthostat there is a low stone perhaps like the buttress-stone intended to support the gallery side. There are two outer-wall stones alongside some 1.5m beyond the end of the S side of the gallery. A large stone in front of the tomb is displaced. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 73-4, 116, no. 116)

SL038-074----:
The monument, destroyed sometime between 1914 and 1942, stood on rolling pasture about 1km SW of Tobercurry town. A sketch of the tomb by Wakeman (1878-82, drawing book 1, folio 109) and a plan by Wood-Martin (1886-7, 276; 1888, 214) show a dual court tomb, aligned more or less E-W, consisting of two two-chambered galleries set back to back and 3.8m apart. Two sidestones on each side, the southern segmenting jamb and the backstone of the western gallery were then in place as were four sidestones to the S, one to the N, the northern segmenting jamb and the backstone of the eastern gallery. An OS 1:2500 field trace (1914) depicts two galleries aligned NE-SW within a roughly rectangular enclosure which seems to represent a mound (L 25m; Wth 15m). (Ó Nualláin 1989, 74-5, no. 118)

SL040-006001-:
(In the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery). On a spur on the northern slopes of Kesh Corann and commanding an extensive outlook to the N. A NE-facing passage tomb (L 5m) stands towards the N end of a ruined circular cairn (diam. 19m; H c. 0.5m). Some kerbstones at the W side of the cairn and one or two possible examples at the E indicate an original diameter of c. 15m. Eight orthostats form the more easterly side of the tomb. There are four, possibly five, in situ at the opposite side and it is closed by a substantial backstone. An in-turn of the more easterly side divides the tomb into an inner (L 3m; max. Wth 1.5m) and outer (L 2m) compartment. A large roofstone (max. dim. 2.5m) is in place above the inner compartment. A much smaller stone wedged between the forward end of the last and the more westerly side of the tomb may be a displaced roofstone. A large slab (max. dim. 2.1m) leans against the outer face of the more westerly side of the outer compartment and would seem to be a displaced roofstone. Ten or more relatively small slabs lie displaced at the site. In 1993 a small pocket of cremated bone, apparently a secondary deposition, found near the kerb was later identified as the remains of one adult (Buckley and Mount 1994, 71). An enclosure (SL040-00602-) lies immediately to S. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 84)

SL040-008----:
(In the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery). On the summit of Kesh Corann with a magnificent outlook in all directions. Within and close to the N edge of a hilltop enclosure (SL040-009---). This is a circular cairn (diam. 26m; H c. 4-5m) at the top of which there is a small pile of stones, apparently a 19th-century OS trigonometrical station. A hole (4m x 3m; D 0.5m) has been dug into the E slope of the cairn and there is a larger hole extending from the summit downslope to the ENE. The cairn stands on what appears to be a prepared platform (diam. c. 35m), the perimeter of which is almost 5m beyond the base of the cairn. The platform is now substantially grass-grown and in places, especially at the N, peat-grown. It is c. 0.8m high around the greater part of the perimeter but reaches 2m high at the N over falling ground. Kerbstones are intermittently visible along or just inside the platform perimeter, in particular on the southern side. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 84)

In the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. At the northern extremity of a N-S ridge. The cairn, part of the N end of which has slipped over the end of the ridge on which it sits, is of oval plan (18m N-S; 23m E-W; H 2.5m). Some piled stones on the top of the cairn may be a 19th-century OS trigononmetrical station. A small number of kerbstones are intermittently visible around the southern half of the perimeter. A substantially rubble-filled chamber is partly exposed in a hole in the eastern half of the cairn. This consists of two opposed orthostats, 0.7m apart, aligned E-W, which support a roofstone (min. L 2m; Wth 0.8m; T 0.25m). The nature of this chamber is uncertain but it could be the remains of a passage tomb. A short cist (SL040-016002-) was uncovered just inside the W edge of the cairn (Rynne 1969). (Ó Nualláin 1989, 84)

This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). Carn C in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. On the bog-grown northern slopes of the Bricklieve Mountains and 10m N of possible passage tomb (SL040-087----). A circular cairn (diam. 17-19m; H 1.5m) with a slight bulge at the W where there has been some slippage downslope, is crossed by a field boundary wall. Just W of the centre of the mound there is the remains of a passage (L 3m; Wth c. 0.5m) opening to the WNW. A massive lintel covers the inner end of the passage. Beyond this the N or left-hand side and rear of the chamber area is represented by tiered corbelling which extends for a further 3m to the ESE. At about mid-length the line of corbelling bulges to the N indicating the possible presence of a side recess. The corbelling rises above a substantial body of fill that hides the orthostatic structure. Some 1.2m to the S of the line of the passage and more or less opposite the northwards bulge already referred to, a roofed polygonal chamber (max. dims. 1.7m x 1.7m) is accessible from the top of the cairn. The field wall crossing the monument separates this chamber from the rest of the tomb structure and obscures their relationship but it would seem that this is a recess opening off the right-hand side of the chamber area at the end of the passage. Two orthostats form the E and W sides of this chamber and a single example closes the S end. At the northern end there are three stones arranged in the manner of a doorstone between two jambs which support a lintel now partly displaced. The design here supports the likelihood of a connection between this chamber and the structure to the N of the field wall. The roofstone of this chamber is somewhat precariously supported on a single layer of corbels, including the lintel just mentioned. The design of this tomb is uncertain but the indications are that it is cruciform in plan (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 322-3; Ó Nualláin 1989, 82)

SL040-089----:
This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). Carn G in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. High on the N slope of Barrnabinnia, one of the bog-grown N-S aligned ridges forming the Bricklieve Mountains. A possible passage tomb (SL040-088----) lies c. 40m to NW and a passage tomb (SL040-09001-) c. 50m to S. A circular cairn (diam. 18-20m; H 3m) covers a well-preserved cruciform passage tomb opening to the NW. The tomb (L 5m) consists of a passage (L 2m; Wth c. 1m) leading to a chamber (L 1.7m; Wth 1.9m; H 2.3m) opening off which there are two opposed side-chambers, one to the right or W (L 0.85m; Wth 0.95m; H 1.3m), another to the left or E (L 0.85m; Wth 1.1m; H 1.4m) and an endchamber (L 1m; Wth 1m; H 1.3m). The tomb is constructed of tall, generally pillar-like uprights and these support a series of lintels and oversailing corbels capped by a large flat slab above the main chamber. Sillstones divide the passage into two compartments and are in place at the front of the two side-chambers and endchamber. Investigation of the tomb in 1911 (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 327-8, 334-5) showed that large flat slabs (some of which are still visible) had been laid as floorstones along the passage and in the chambers. The tomb contained a considerable quantity of burnt bone, some pottery fragments, stone pendants, beads and balls. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 83)

SL040-090001-:
Carn H in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. About 50m S of and slightly upslope from another passage tomb (SL040-089----). A circular cairn (diam. 20m; H 2.5m), inside the perimeter of which there is a quite well-preserved kerb (diam. 14m), contains a NW-facing undifferentiated passage tomb. Only the outer half of the passage is now accessible. In 1911 (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 328-9, 335) a slab at the entrance and the outermost roofstone were broken up and removed to allow access. However it was not possible to crawl all the way along the narrow passage so entry to the chamber at the end of the passage was gained by quarrying through the top of the cairn and raising roofstones. This part of the tomb, now covered by cairn slip, is inaccessible. The published plan (ibid.) shows the passage (which is slightly curved) and chamber to be some 8.5m long. The outer third of the structure is at most 1m high and wide and it would seem that the chamber at the inner end is of comparable dimensions. The middle part of the structure narrows to about 0.5m. The orthostats of the outer part of the passage are unequal in height so drystone-walling is employed to provide a reasonably level surface for the roofing lintels. Two jamb-like stones seem to mark a point of segmentation about 1m from the entrance and the published plan (ibid.) shows three sillstones further along, one of them dividing the passage from the chamber. Finds at the site consisted of burnt and unburnt bones, a stone bead and a sea-shell. A stretch of field boundary (T 4m; H 0.4-0.5m) (SL040-090002-) composed of stone rubble and slabs laid lengthways extends from the W side of the passage tomb into the bog. A megalithic structure (SL040-091----) lies c. 30m to SE. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 83)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). Carn K in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. About 130m S of and somewhat upslope from the megalithic structure (SL040-091----), 10m E of a possible passage tomb (SL040-094----) and c. 400m N of another passage tomb (SL040-101----). A round cairn (diam. 21.5-23m; H 3.5m) covers a well-preserved cruciform passage tomb opening to the NNW. The tomb (L 7.7m) consists of a passage (L 4.5m; Wth 0.65-1.1m) leading to a chamber (L 1.4m; Wth 1.9m; H 3.4m) opening off which there are two opposed side-chambers, one to the right or W (L 1.35m; Wth 1.4m; H 2.2m), another to the left or E (L 1m; Wth 1.2m; H 2.1m) and an endchamber (L 1m; Wth 1.4m; H 2m). The tomb is constructed of orthostats with dry-wall infill which support a series of lintels, a number now cracked, and oversailing corbels capped by a large flat slab above the main chamber. Sillstones divide the passage into three sections and are in place at the front of the two side-chambers and endchamber. Investigation of the tomb in 1911 (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 329) produced burnt bones, stone pendants, beads and balls, mushroom and poppy-headed antler and bone pins, and a decorated Bronze Age bowl (Ó Riordáin and Waddell 1993, 130). There is a cist (SL040-092----) c. 20m to NE. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 83)

This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). Carn E in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. On the bog-covered cliff-walled northern tip of one of the N-S aligned ridges that form the Bricklieve Mountains. Another passage tomb (SL040-096----) lies 200m to S. A long cairn (L 40m; min. H 2m), its perimeter partly obscured by heather-grown bog, is aligned NNW-SSE. Visible kerbstones indicate a max. width of 11m at the S. Close to the N end of the cairn there is a cruciform passage tomb. This consists of a NNW-facing main chamber (L 4m; min. Wth 0.6m, max. Wth 1.35m) divided by sills into four compartments. Opposed side-chambers, both polygonal in outline, and both c. 1m by 0.7m in dimension, open off the taller main chamber. Four orthostats are in place on each side of the main chamber and a fifth example has collapsed inwards at the inner end of the E side. Six orthostats form the sides and back of the well-preserved eastern side-chamber which is entered from the main chamber over a sillstone. Four orthostats are in place around the sides and back of the western side-chamber. Each side-chamber is roofed by a single large slab supported on corbelling. A slab laid lintel-like on the outer pair of opposed sidestones of the main chamber is a modern feature. Immediately in front of the main chamber there is a tall stone which projects outwards from the line of the E side of the structure. This stone and at least three other large stones which seem to be displaced to a lesser or greater degree suggest there may have been further structure at this end of the tomb. Bone fragments, a minute sherd of pottery, a poppy-headed and a mushroom-headed pin and portion of a boar's tusk were recovered from the tomb in 1911 (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 323-4, 332-3). At the southern end of the cairn there is a setting of stones which has been compared to a court (Ó Nualláin 1989, 75-6, no. 120, 82). If, as appears to be the case, it opened onto the end of the cairn it would have measured 5m N-S and almost the same dimension E-W. A large orthostat (L 3.3m) forms the inner end of this feature, there are two on its more westerly side and one on the opposite side. Some 2.5m NE of the court-like feature there is a small chamber opening onto the E side of the cairn. Two pairs of opposed sidestones are visible at the front of this chamber (min. L 1.5m). A roofstone and three corbels, all now partly displaced apparently due to the investigation of the site in 1911 (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 323-4, 332-3), obscure the rear of the chamber.

This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). Carn F in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. Close to the western edge of a heather-covered bog-grown ridge and 200m S of another passage tomb (SL040-095----) on the same ridge. A largely collapsed N-facing passage tomb (L 6.2m) is partly exposed towards the N side of a round cairn (diam. 29m; H 5.5m). The site was investigated in 1911 (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 324-7, 333-4) by which stage it was in a state of partial collapse. The upper part of the roof had given way causing the chamber area to fill with stones from the cairn. Clearance revealed a short passage leading to two pairs of side-chambers and a terminal chamber. Sillstones divided the passage into two compartments and stood at the front of each side-chamber. A standing stone, its butt still in place and upper part prostrate alongside, stood between the inner pair of transepts and in front of the terminal chamber. The roof, constructed of oversailing corbels, is estimated to have been some 5m high. It had been capped with a large slab which lay displaced on the cairn in 1911. In the course of clearance this stone was broken up and removed. Some corbels became displaced during the work and were also removed. Finds recovered all came from the inner end of the structure and included some burnt bone, a complete bead and two broken examples. During the 1911 investigation the stone fill from the inner part of the tomb was moved to the front which had already been cleared. This material and further cairn collapse since 1911 now covers most of the orthostatic structure including the side-chambers. At the front four stones, two at either side forming the outer end of passage, and at the other end the tops of three orthostats, the backstone and the sidestone adjoining either end of it, are now visible. Two lintels are exposed near the front of the passage. Three overlying corbels rest on the backstone and these support a roofstone at the rear of the tomb. Corbels are exposed along the length of the structure. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 83)
