SL040-097001-:
Carn B in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. At the cliff-walled northern extremity of one of the N-S aligned ridges that form the Bricklieve Mountains. This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). A N-facing undifferentiated passage tomb, exposed in 1911 (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 321-3), stands towards the northern end of a circular cairn (diam. 27m; max. H 5m). Around the southern half of the perimeter and half way down the cairn there are traces of the internal revetment of a drystone wall (ibid.). Surviving kerbstones indicate an original cairn diameter of 23m. The roofed chamber measures 2.85m from a sillstone at the front to the backstone. It widens from 0.6m at the front to 1.25m at the rear and increases in height from some 0.9m to c. 1.5m. Two further sillstones divide it into three compartments, the innermost slightly longer and also wider than the others. The innermost sillstone stands between two jamb-like stones set inside the chamber walls. It would seem that this feature is incorrectly surveyed on the published plan (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, Pl. 17) and interpreted as a cist. Passage tomb art has been discovered on the N jambstone and adjacent orthostat (Hensey and Robin 2012). Three large slabs roof the tomb. The published plan shows a recess to the right of the sillstone at the front of the tomb. It does seem that this is not an original feature but the result of partial collapse. Immediately forward of the front sill there are two opposed slabs, the bases of both exposed, and each apparently deliberately propped against the outer ends of the sides of the tomb. Their status is uncertain. During the 1911 investigation burnt human bone and some pottery fragments were found in the tomb and two short cists (SL040-097002-), apparently secondary, were uncovered on the E side of the cairn of the passage tomb. A cashel (SL040-082001-) and field wall (SL040-082002-) lie c. 80m to W. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 82)

On a little knoll in rocky pasture at the foot of the E flank of the Bricklieve Mountains. This is a gallery (L 6.3m; Wth 2m at front, 0.8m at rear) entered between two jambs at the NW, the more easterly of which is flanked by a single courtstone. There are three stones on the W side of the gallery and four on the E and it is closed by a backstone the top of which has been broken off and now lies on the ground. The gallery contains grass-grown fill which reaches to the level of the sidestones and this extends beyond the front of the monument for about 1.5m. A slab, apparently a roofstone, rests on this fill at the back of the gallery. A stone fence runs E-W across the middle of the gallery. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 75, no. 119)

This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). Carn O in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. At the northern end of Doonaveeragh, the easternmost of the N-S aligned ridges forming the Bricklieve Mountains. A circular cairn (diam. 18-20m; H 2.5m), its lower levels grass-grown, contains towards its southern end a partly roofed chamber (L 2m; max. Wth 0.8m; H 0.9m). Built of orthostats and dry-wall infill, a narrowing of the chamber indicates a division into a shorter and narrower compartment, now roofless, to the S and a slightly wider and longer northern compartment, roofed by two slabs, one overlying the other. Both ends of the chamber are closed. It was investigated in 1911 (Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger 1912, 330, 336-7) when entry was gained through the roof. A decorated Bronze Age bowl was found within the chamber, resting on a pile of burnt and unburnt bones intermixed with small sandstone slabs (ibid.; Ó Riordáin and Waddell 1993,130). There is a Neolithic settlement (SL040-108----) on the lower ground to N. A cairn (SL040-100----) lies c. 200m to SSE. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 83-4)

This is a National Monument in State care (no. 518). Carn M in the Carrowkeel-Kesh Corann passage tomb cemetery. About 400m S of a passage tomb K (SL040-093----) and a possible passage tomb (SL040-094----) and c. 80m N of another passage tomb (SL040-102----) on the N edge of a small plateau with views limited to local horizons. A small, roofless, NW-facing cruciform passage tomb rises clear of a substantially grass-grown circular cairn (diam. c. 10m; H 1m). A passage (L 1m; Wth 0.7m) is separated by a sill from a central space (L c. 0.8m; Wth c. 0.6m) opening off which are two opposed side-chambers, one to the right (L c. 1m; Wth c. 0.9m), another to the left (L c. 0.8m; Wth 0.4m) and an endchamber (L c. 0.8m; Wth 0.4m). None of the tomb orthostats exceeds 0.8m in height. Some slabs lie prostrate on the mound forward of the passage which according to Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger (1912, 330) was originally 10 feet (c. 3m) long. A small excavation of the cairn (Bergh 1987, 32) led to the recovery of human bone at the edge of the tomb. Radiocarbon dating of a human tooth yielded a date in the interval 2451 to 2039 cal BC and of charcoal a date in the interval 3370 to 3042 cal BC (Bergh 1995, 105). (Ó Nualláin 1989, 83)

SL040-107----:
In rough, heather-covered upland pasture in the Bricklieve Mountains, located in a shallow natural hollow on the E side of a broad plateau on top of a NNE−SSW ridge. The stone stands close to the break of slope on the E side of the ridge where ground falls away steeply into a narrow valley. It is overlooked immediately to S by a higher level of the ridge top. Upright block of limestone (H c. 2m; L 1.73m NE−SW at base; T max. c. 1.05m at base) which narrows from a broad base to a pointed top, giving the stone a pronounced triangular shape. The stone has a rough surface, partly colonised by lichen, moss and grass. There are two passage tombs (SL040-101----; SL040-102----) on a parallel ridge to E; it is possible that these were visible in the past from the stone but they are now low, heather-covered mounds and cannot be seen. Two other passage tombs (SL040-095----; SL040-096----) are located on ridge tops c. 440m to NNW and 340m to NW respectively, but are not visible from the standing stone.
Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

SL040-127----:
On a low ridge close to the W shore of Lough Arrow. The tomb stands in a low oval mound (25.5m SSE-NNW; 9m ENE-WSW). A court (min. L 5m) to the SSE is represented by four stones, one at the outer and one at the inner ends of both arms. Two jambs mark the entrance to a gallery (L 8m), a segmenting jamb on the N side of which indicates a division into two chambers. One stone remains of the N side of the first chamber and there are two on the S side. A stone outside the inner of these two seems to represent a doubling of the gallery side. Two orthostats at the S are the only remains of the inner chamber. A large slab in the front chamber may be a lintel displaced from above the entrance jambs. There is also a displaced slab at the back of the gallery.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

SL040-184----:
On a flat tract of ground, on the slopes below the S end of the Bricklieve Mountains with an outlook to the SE across Lough Key. A lone orthostat (L 1.2m; T 0.2m; H 0.75m), aligned SW-NE, stands at about the centre of an oval mound (L 22.5m NE-SW; max. Wth 16m; max. H 1.5m). Immediately to the S of the surviving orthostat there is a prostrate slab and just beyond this another measuring (max. dims. 1.1m and 2.2m respectively). Some 3m to the WSW of the orthostat three small stones, none more than 0.3m high, form a slightly curved line (L 2m). A fence runs NNW-SSE across the mound near its eastern edge. There is a small pit in the mound at the SE and another at the SW. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 77, no. 122)

SL040-229----:
In pasture on an E-facing terrace on the northern slopes of the Bricklieve Mountains and commanding a view over Lough Arrow 1.6 km to the E. The scant remains of a structure, possibly a chamber (L 2.2m) aligned NW-SE, stand in a mound of subrectangular plan (8.5m NE-SW; 8m NW-SE; H 0.4m). To the NW two opposed orthostats, the taller 0.7m high, stand 1.2m apart at either side of a low stone, possibly a sill, set transversely between them. These stones may mark the front of a chamber that appears to be closed by a stone (H 0.6m) some 2.2m to the SE of and parallel to the sillstone. Another stone (H 0.65m) is set face on to the NW end of the more northerly of the opposed orthostats. A partly buried stone immediately alongside the outer face of the more southerly of the opposed orthostats is not definitely structural. There are three prostrate stones at the site, the largest 1.75m in max. dimension. Enclosure (SL040-03201-) c. 150m to SSE.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

SL040-234----:
On a slight terrace on the S slope of Kesh Corann and commanding an extensive outlook to the S. This is a W-facing gallery (L 6m) which decreases in height to the E. There is a jamb-like stone at the W end of the gallery. This articulates with the N side of the structure which is now represented by at least six partly concealed orthostats. A low backstone closes the E end of the gallery. Its S side is concealed by a spread of stones and may have collapsed. A low orthostat outside the N end of the backstone may be a buttress-stone. Some 1.5m S of the backstone there are two low stones. These seem to be the remains of an outer wall. There are some remains of mound around the S half of the structure.

SL041-004----:
In a small valley, on pasture broken by limestone outcrops. A gallery (L 5.2m; Wth c. 1m) is segmented by jambs into two chambers. The entrance, at the NE, is marked by a pair of jambs but no evidence for a court survives. Single stones form the sides of the chambers and the rear of the gallery. A roofstone, apparently broken, covers part of the inner chamber. A low field bank extends N-S across the front of the gallery. There is a low mound (14m NW-SE; 9m NE-SW) around the sides and back of the gallery. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 77-8, no. 123)

SL041-034001-:
In gently sloping rocky pasture. A ruined gallery (L 4.5m; Wth 2.2m) is aligned NE-SW. A prostrate stone at the NE end is a fallen backstone (Wood-Martin 1883-4, 448-9, no. 2; 1888, 169, no. 2). Three orthostats are in place at the more northerly side. Two are alongside to the W and are separated by a gap 1.3m wide from the third which adjoins the prostrate backstone. One orthostat is in place at the NE end of the other side of the gallery. Alongside to the W there is another orthostat that has fallen outwards and is now almost prostrate. The outer end of the last supports a stone, possibly a displaced orthostat (ibid.). A natural oval hillock (SL041-034002-) at the edge of the field c. 100m to SE is possibly what Wood-Martin (1883-4, 449) referred to as a 'sepulchral mound on the summit of a slight rise almost obliterated by tillage'. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 78, no. 124)

SL044-045----:
In undulating pasture and incorporated into a stone field boundary. An upright lozenge-shaped limestone stone (H 1.6m; Wth 1.65m; T 0.5m), split in two from top to bottom; several small stones have been placed into the resulting fracture. It was recorded in 1836 as 'Cloch mor na creagadh, Big stone of the Creggs. Creagadh is the name of the ground on which it stands' (OSNB vol. 1, 433).

SL044-051----:
Almost 1km W of the N end of Lough Gara on a patch of rocky pasture in gently rolling land. The remains of a court (min. L 6m; Wth c. 8m at its inner end) at the NW, its more westerly arm represented by four stones and the opposite arm by two, opens into two galleries set side by side. Little remains of the more westerly gallery (min. L 7m) the entrance to which is formed by two jambs. A sidestone abuts the more easterly of these and there is another on the same side almost 4m to the S. Opposite this there is another sidestone and between them what appears to be a segmenting jamb. Its presence indicates there was further gallery structure here. The second gallery (min. L 6.5m) consists of an antechamber represented by the more easterly entrance jamb and a sidestone abutting it. Segmenting jambs separate this from a chamber the E side of which is represented by a single stone and the W side by two stones. Another pair of segmenting jambs stand between the last and another chamber, its intact W side of two stones and two of a likely original three stones in place at the E. A segmenting jamb adjoins the outer end of the W side of this indicating that there was at least one further chamber here. There are some displaced stones at the site. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 79-80, no. 126)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

SL044-057----:
In gently undulating pasture with good views. An upright sandstone slab (H 2.15m; 1.14m x 0.47m; long axis NNE-SSW) leaning to NW. They were recorded in 1836 as 'two standing stones near each other, both called Cloghmore of Doon.' (OSNB vol. 1, 435).

SL044-062----:
In a small isolated patch of unreclaimed bog in rolling pasture about 5km W of the N end of Lough Gara. The tomb, much of which is either missing or remains concealed in the bog, faces W and protrudes from a heel-shaped mound (L 9m E-W; max. Wth 7.5m at W). The forward 2.6m of the gallery is visible. Opposed stones, 1.45m apart, form the gallery entrance. A single sidestone adjoins the southern of these and 0.6m beyond this a partly concealed stone may be a fallen orthostat. Two orthostats adjoin the northern entrance stone. Outside these there are two stones that serve to double the gallery wall at this point. A lintel that covered the entrance has slipped off the S side of the gallery. Broken lines of outer-walling to the N and S join a facade running across the W end of the tomb. Two facade-stones link the S side of the gallery entrance to the outer-wall and these articulate with a line of three outer-wall stones, each of which has fallen outwards. The surviving facade-stone at the N articulates with the front of the outer-walling at this side of the monument. It adjoins a line of five stones, the middle three fallen outwards and the easternmost partly buried. Another outer-wall stone stands some 2.3m to the E. A small set stone 2.3m S of the last is of uncertain function. Three displaced stones lie on the mound at the NE. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 78-9, no. 125)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

SL046-010----:
On level ground, on a slight dry rise in otherwise waterlogged ground. A boulder (1.8m x 1.5m; T 0.7m) rests on three support-stones. The two most northerly support-stones are each 0.35m H while the southerly stone is 0.25m H. Above the lowest support-stone is a pad-stone which serves to steady the cover-stone above its supports (Ó Nualláin 1986, 124).

SL046-035----:
On rolling pasture about 600m W of Lough Gara. A W-facing gallery (min. L 6.7m) is divided by a septal-stone into a portico and main chamber and is surrounded by the remains of an outer-wall. The structure, which is built with quite small orthostats, stands in a low mound (10m E-W; max. 8m N-S; H 0.5m). The portico (L 1.5m) is formed by two stones at the S and another, now fallen, at the N side. The septal-stone is broken in two pieces. Between the N end of the septal-stone and the N side of the main chamber there is a small stone. The main chamber (min. L 5m; Wth 1.2m at septal-stone, 0.9m towards opposite end) is represented by six stones to the N and five to the S. At the inner end of the S side there is a partly buried stone of uncertain function. There is a displaced stone about mid-way along the main chamber. The outer-wall at the N is represented by seven stones and that at the S also by seven stones. A partly buried stone immediately outside the easternmost outer-wall stone at the S seems to be prostrate. The back of the outer-walling is represented by a single orthostat. Two facade-stones, both fallen to W, linked the southern outer-wall to the front of the portico. A single facade-stone, a thin slab, stands just forward of the northern outer-wall. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 80-81, no. 127)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

An upright flat-topped limestone slab (H 1.35m; Wth 0.72m; T 0.38m; long-axis NW-SE), rectangular in plan and tapering towards the top (Wth 0.07m). It is used as a scratching post by cattle resulting in polished edges and a slight depression around the base. A possible cashel (SL046-024----) is c. 100m to SW.
